job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts in my parents' flat above their takeaway on Station Road. Mum and Dad open at eleven, so in the morning I do applications and keep the shop's online orders running, which is my unpaid IT job. In the afternoon I do a coding challenge or a certification module, and from five till ten I'm behind the counter or on deliveries. I fall asleep with the job alerts open.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what has the search looked like so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer science with a networking focus and finished with a good result in June. My final project was a network traffic monitor that flags odd behaviour, and I did a three-month placement on the IT helpdesk at the county council. Since then I've sent around eighty applications, had three interviews and heard nothing back from two of them. I have heavy student debt, about a month of costs saved if I stop eating well, and my parents can't help because the takeaway barely breaks even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, I never believed the wildest stories. I'd tell friends who panicked that we should wait and see rather than rearrange our lives. I'd also say that we still have the same problem as before, which is that junior roles are scarce and everyone asks for experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau is neutral on paper but heavy for me. My search is slow because there aren't many IT jobs near us, and the council helpdesk where I did my placement only hires through an agency. Debt keeps growing, and the takeaway is getting less busy since delivery apps took a bigger cut. So nothing shifts, and nothing improves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, and I'd widen to help-desk and support jobs even though I'd hoped for something more technical. I'd take the cloud certification I've been studying, which costs about two hundred pounds. I'd ask my placement manager, Ms Brennan, for a reference and maybe a contact at the agency. And I'd keep working evenings at the shop, since that's money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient, and a bit stuck between two lives, one at the counter and one in front of the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a plateau change the takeaway, if at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Delivery apps took twenty-five percent of every order, and Dad is getting tired of it. If AI makes ordering or the till a little easier, great, but the margins won't change. We might lose one part-time driver. So the shop's income gets tighter, and I'm the unpaid backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you doing that gives you any edge over other graduates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm patient, I do the unglamorous bits, and I actually fix things for real people, like the shop's wifi, the printer and the online menu. Employers like hearing that, I think. And I'm willing to take a helpdesk job to get started, where some of my classmates insist on a software role.

say: I'd tell panicking friends to **wait** and see rather than rearrange our lives.
Junior roles are still scarce and everyone asks for experience.
think: A plateau is neutral on paper but **heavy** for me, since debt keeps growing and local IT jobs are few.
The takeaway's margins are shrinking because of delivery apps.
do: Widen applications to **helpdesk** and support jobs, not just technical ones.
Finish the cloud certification, which costs about two hundred pounds.
Ask Ms Brennan for a reference and an agency contact, and keep working evenings at the shop.
feel: **Impatient**, stuck between the counter and the screen.
S0.quote: I'm willing to take a helpdesk job to get started, where some of my classmates insist on a software role.
fieldNote: He is **pragmatic**, willing to take lower-status IT work as a start.
The family takeaway is shrinking, so he carries both **debt** and the shop's problems.
His real edge is fixing things for real people, which employers like.

steps.text: Apply for helpdesk and IT support jobs across the county
Ask Ms Brennan for a reference and agency contact
Keep working evenings at the family takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and it's coming steadily, so we should deal with it calmly. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and not wait for a company to teach them. I'd also say the government should help firms train juniors, because otherwise this just hits the youngest people hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Helpdesk work is answering customers, checking and booking, which is exactly the list on the card. At the council, I answered about forty tickets a day and most were password resets or printer problems, and a chatbot can do those. So my entry route is the part that shrinks first. At the same time, someone needs to manage the systems that do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools more now, because I only use them now and then, mostly for debugging. I'd aim for roles in network or cloud support, where you need to understand what's under the chatbot. I'd also build a small project showing I can set up and monitor an AI helper for a small shop, using our takeaway as the test case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, a bit gloomy. It feels like picking a path that is already half-paved over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would software change the helpdesk where you did your placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably keep a few people for the strange problems and let a chatbot take the rest. Before, there were six of us on the desk, and I can see it being two. The junior seat, where you learn how the network really works, is exactly the one that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you pick a different path from helpdesk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go toward the plumbing, networks, security, cloud setup. It's less glamorous but someone has to keep the thing running. Another option is helping small businesses like Dad's set up simple tools, because they can't afford a big firm. That could be a real small business for me.

say: I'd tell friends to **learn** the tools and not wait for a company to teach them.
Government should help firms train juniors so the youngest don't take the hit.
think: Helpdesk is answering customers and booking, so my **entry route** shrinks first.
Someone still has to manage the systems doing the work.

Aim for network or cloud support roles that sit under the chatbots.
Build a small project setting up an AI helper for our takeaway.
feel: Like picking a path that is already half-paved over.
S1.quote: The junior seat, where you learn how the network really works, is exactly the one that goes.
fieldNote: His council **placement** gives him concrete numbers: six on the desk, maybe two later.
He finds a path in the plumbing of IT, which is steadier than front-line support.
Helping small shops like his family's could become a **small business**.

steps.text: Aim applications at network and cloud support roles
Use AI tools daily for coding and debugging practice
Build an AI order helper for the family takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to hit everyone, and we need government to take the lead. I'd say it plainly, without drama. We need support for people who lose work, training that's actually paid, and a clear plan from companies, because two years is hardly any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm very afraid. IT is the first thing to be eaten. Two years from now I'd be a fresh graduate in a field where a machine does the whole job, cheaper and faster. And I wouldn't have the savings to retrain for months. My degree turns from an asset into a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I could get, whatever it is, and I'd stay with my parents. I'd stop spending on the certification and put any money in a savings account. I'd look for jobs that put me close to people, like hospital support, a trade apprenticeship or even working at the council's front desk. And I'd learn to fix machines, since robots will need repairing a few years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. My stomach drops every time I think of the year 2028. It feels like the end date has been written on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents the night it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down at the kitchen table and tell them straight. They'd listen and say it will be okay, because that's what parents say, but Dad would go quiet. They'd want me to stay close, and I'd stay, because there's a shop to help run and no money to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the takeaway, would it make it through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. A takeaway is hands-on, but customers will order through whatever's cheapest, and delivery apps or AI ordering would swallow the margin. The cooking is hands-on and would last longer, though. We'd survive on being local, and people knowing Dad.

say: I'd say plainly that government must lead, with **paid** training and support for people who lose work.
Two years is hardly any time.
think: IT is eaten first, so my degree turns from an asset into a **bill**.
I wouldn't have the savings to retrain for months.
do: Take the **first** job I can get and stay with my parents.
Stop paying for the certification and save any money instead.
Look for jobs near people, such as hospital support or a trade apprenticeship.
feel: **Heavy**, with my stomach dropping at the year 2028.
The end date feels written on the wall.
S2.quote: My degree turns from an asset into a bill.
fieldNote: He talks about **fear** calmly, which hides how alarmed he is.
Family loyalty is his anchor, with the shop as a reason to stay near home.
He considers **people-facing** work that machines reach later.

steps.text: Take the first IT or support job offered
Stop the certification fees and save the money
Look into hospital support or trade apprenticeships
Stay at home with my parents and help at the takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to build a plan but not enough to waste. I'd tell people to stay calm and start acting sensibly, like building skills and saving. I'd push for training schemes and some sort of income cushion, which I'd call fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's much better than two years. I could get a job, save a bit and have three or four years of experience. But I'd be the junior in a field where seniors might still be needed, and juniors might not. So I'd aim to become the person who manages the systems, not just uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job in IT support or networks, anything, and stay at it for two years while saving a third of my pay. I'd study security, because it's the part where firms still want human judgement, and I'd learn to repair hardware, as a back-up. I'd keep helping at the shop but only evenings, so it doesn't take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. I'd say I'm about a quarter less scared, and I notice that. Like, I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different when you have five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's friend Mr Rahim, who owns a small computer repair shop. He doesn't have much money, but he knows everyone and does hands-on work. I'd ask if I could work there a day a week to learn repairs, and I'd tell him I'd be fine with low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still a gamble, but a better one. At two years, it's a flip of a coin. At five, it's something I can aim at. I have a good degree and I've been steady, and I think that counts for more over five years than over two.

say: I'd say five years is enough to build a plan but not to **waste**.
I'd push for training schemes and an income cushion.
think: Five years is much better than two, but juniors may go before **seniors** do.
I'd aim to be the person who manages the systems.
do: Take any IT support or network job and save a **third** of my pay for two years.
Study security, where firms still want human judgement, and learn hardware repair.
Ask Mr Rahim at the repair shop for a day a week.
S3.quote: At two years, it's a flip of a coin. At five, it's something I can aim at.
fieldNote: He measures his fear, **a quarter less**, which shows a practical, numerate mind.
Mr Rahim is a contact outside his degree who offers real repair experience.
He keeps the shop to **evenings** so it does not swallow his career.

steps.text: Take any IT support or network job and stay two years
Save a third of each pay cheque
Work one day a week at Mr Rahim's repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time to prepare and I'd treat it as a headstart. I'd tell my friends to carry on, get experience and watch what happens in the middle years. I'd also say schools and colleges should start adding practical AI skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm much calmer, though I won't pretend the debt isn't there. With a decade I could get a first job, work my way up and pick up a second skill. By 2036 I'd be thirty-six with ten years of work behind me, and I'd have a decent view of where things are going. I like those odds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job, pay the loan down in the first five years, and learn something new each year, security, cloud, maybe project management. I'd try to move into a role that mixes IT with real businesses, like helping shops or small clinics. And I'd save for a flat deposit instead of a rainy-day pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some nerves. I'd put it at about a three out of ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what degree you'd have picked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still pick computer science, but I'd add something with business or healthcare. A pure tech degree with nothing else is thin. A degree plus knowing how a clinic or a shop runs is much better. I'd tell my cousins that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay it down quickly, because it's the one thing that stays the same whatever the world does. I'd put forty percent of every raise into it. If AI happens as the card says, the people with no debt will have more freedom to choose, and that's what I'd want.

say: I'd treat ten years as a **headstart** and tell friends to get experience while watching the middle years.
Colleges should add practical AI skills now.
think: I'm much **calmer**, though the debt is still there.
By 2036 I'd have ten years of work and a decent view of where things are going.
do: Take a job, pay the loan down in the first five years, and learn a new skill **yearly**.
Move toward a role mixing IT with real businesses like small clinics.
feel: About a three out of ten on worry.
S4.quote: If AI happens as the card says, the people with no debt will have more freedom to choose, and that's what I'd want.
fieldNote: Ten years turns him into a **planner** who sets loan targets, such as forty percent of raises.
He plans to pair tech with knowledge of **businesses** or healthcare.
He is steady, not bold: a three out of ten on worry.

steps.text: Pay forty percent of every raise into the student loan
Learn one new skill a year, such as security or cloud
Move toward roles that support small clinics and shops
Save toward a flat deposit once the loan is smaller

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to get a job and no money to change course. What would help is a clear plan from government and firms, honest and early, not vague promises. Also a way to put the loan on hold when work is missing, a first-job scheme for graduates, and training that doesn't cost me a month's savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume graduates have it easy. I came out of a degree to find that the entry-level step is missing, and my family business is shrinking too. I'd like readers to know that behind the number of applications there's someone working the counter and doing the code at midnight.

headlineQuote: Behind the number of applications there's someone working the counter and doing the code at midnight.
portrait: Wei is a **23-year-old** computer science graduate living above his parents' takeaway, with eighty applications, three interviews and no offer.
He did a council helpdesk placement and a traffic monitor project, and carries heavy debt with about **one month** saved.
He is a pragmatic centrist who takes support work as a start and uses AI tools only now and then.
His **steady** style means a plan for each picture: networks, security and repair skills, with family close by.
He is anxious in most pictures, alarmed with two years, and only uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because there is no time to get a job and no money to change course.
whatWouldHelp: A clear, early **plan** from government and firms, a loan pause when work is missing, and a first-job scheme.
